claims.text: The dynamic mechanical response of solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn is governed by competition between conventional dislocation glide and TRIP mediated by deformation-induced stacking faults.
Higher strain rates reduce dislocation mobility in FeNiCrMn.
Lower temperatures reduce dislocation mobility in FeNiCrMn.
Reduced dislocation mobility causes dislocation accumulation and pile-ups that increase local stress.
Dislocation pile-ups trigger deformation-induced stacking-fault formation.
Deformation-induced stacking faults serve as nucleation sites for a phase transformation and thereby activate TRIP.
TRIP offsets ductility losses associated with high strength and preserves the strength-ductility balance.
As-cast, solidified FeNiCrMn has a primarily FCC microstructure.
The FCC microstructure of as-cast FeNiCrMn is metastable with respect to stacking-fault formation and deformation-induced phase transformation.
High strain rate and low temperature will produce a higher flow stress than the room-temperature, low-rate baseline.
High strain rate and low temperature will produce a more pronounced work-hardening rate than the baseline.
The higher flow stress and work-hardening rate at high rate and low temperature will occur without compromising overall ductility.
At approximately 10^-3 s^-1 and room temperature, dislocation glide dominates and stacking-fault-induced TRIP is minimally active.
Thermomechanical processing that alters stacking-fault energy or phase stability can move FeNiCrMn outside the proposed mechanism's predictive scope.

contradictions.description: A strain rate of approximately 10^-3 s^-1 is called quasi-static in the intervention but is described as a moderate strain rate in the baseline.
